How to use the simulator

1 · Quick start

  1. Click anywhere once so the browser allows alarm sound. Check the top bar shows 🔔 Sound on.
  2. The session opens at design: 366 kNm³/h of make-up syngas joins the recycle gas; circulator C-201 sends 1928 kNm³/h through the four-bed quench converter R-201 at 80 bar g; the effluent is cooled, the crude methanol condenses in separator V-201 and the gas is recycled. About 112.5 t/h of methanol is made (900 kt/y). Open Process to see how it works, P&ID for the drawings, then DCS console to operate it.
  3. Go to Exercises, pick a list (Training, Troubleshooting or Procedures) and click Load. A blue banner gives the situation; click Acknowledge on the banner to hide it.
  4. Operate from the DCS console: click an instrument bubble, a value box or the circulator to open its faceplate on the right. C-201, the E-204 steam block valve, the E-203 cooling water, the blowdown HV-205 and outside checks (lab samples, spare thermocouples, gauge glass) are on the Field tab.
  5. Use Speed to run faster (2×–50×) and Freeze to pause while you think. The beds take 5–15 minutes to settle; inerts in the loop take an hour: use 20× or 50×.
  6. When finished, open Debrief and grading for your score, then Data export to download CSV files for your report.

4 · DCS console

  • Overview: every main loop, the bed temperatures, the converter feed, the loop and a summary at top left.
  • Converter profile: catalyst temperature down each bed (dashed = design) and the CH3OH–temperature diagram: the green equilibrium curve for the gas fed now, the red operating lines of the four beds (calculated from the thermocouples, the quench flows and AIT-208), and the approach to equilibrium of each bed. A bed that touches the green curve stops converting.
  • Quench and interchangers: the cold-shot valves and flows, E-201, E-202, the start-up heater E-204 and the bed exits.
  • Loop: make-up, circulation, pressure, purge, separator, analyzers, carbon efficiency.
  • Profitability: dollars per hour and totals for methanol, make-up gas, purge fuel credit, circulator power, start-up steam and flared gas.

Instrument bubbles follow ISA style: letters on top, loop number below, live value beside it, controller mode (MAN, AUTO) at upper right. Grey value boxes are indicators. A red value is in alarm; a flashing value is not yet acknowledged. Bed colours go from grey-blue (cold) to orange-red (hot).

Trainee workbook · Methanol Converter Ver 1

Work through Parts A to G in order. Record your answers and evidence (screenshots, CSV files) as you go; your report is built from them.

1 Purpose · 2 The unit · 3 Control scheme · 4 Safety systems · 5 Operating rules · 6 Activities A–G · 7 Grading · 8 Report checklist

1 · Purpose

This workbook trains you to operate, monitor and troubleshoot the methanol synthesis converter of a low-pressure methanol plant: an ICI-type quench converter with four adiabatic Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 beds inside a synthesis loop. By the end you should be able to:

  1. Read the P&ID and the DCS displays and state the normal value and alarm limits of every key tag.
  2. Explain, with the CH3OH–temperature diagram, why the reaction stops at equilibrium, why each bed must be quenched, and why the outlet methanol is only about 5 % so the gas must be recycled.
  3. Predict how make-up rate, circulation, loop pressure, bed inlet temperatures, separator temperature and gas composition move the bed temperatures, the purge and the production.
  4. Heat the converter from cold, admit make-up through the SIS and line out; stop it with the catalyst warm; restart it hot.
  5. Recognise an abnormal situation from alarms, trends and field checks, keep the catalyst below its sintering limit, and find the root cause with a systematic six-stage method.
  6. Propose an improvement and support it with exported data.

2 · The unit

Make-up syngas from the front end (FV-202, XV-202; FIC-202) joins the recycle gas at the suction of circulator C-201 (FIC-201 sets its speed). The combined gas is heated in the cold interchanger E-202 to about 97 °C and split: most of it goes to the cold shots TV-221/231/241 (lozenge distributors above beds 2, 3 and 4), the rest is heated in the hot interchanger E-201 (bypass TV-211, TIC-211) and, during start-up only, in the steam heater E-204, and enters bed 1 at 220 °C. Each bed runs adiabatic and rises about 40 °C; the cold shot then resets the next bed inlet. The effluent (about 268 °C, 4.8 % CH3OH) gives its heat back in E-201 and E-202, is cooled to 40 °C in E-203, and the crude methanol condenses in separator V-201 (LIC-204). The gas is recycled; PV-203 purges enough of it to fuel to hold 75 bar g (PIC-203) and to remove inerts.

Values are the model's design point with noise off, for 900 kt/y of methanol (112.5 t/h at 8000 h/y). The reference card gives the reactor type, 220–280 °C, 50–100 bar, Cu/ZnO/Al2O3, GHSV 8000–12 000 h⁻¹ and 900 kt/y; the pressure (80 bar g), make-up composition (H2 73 / CO 16 / CO2 7 / CH4 3.3 / N2 0.5 %), catalyst volume and split, exchanger sizes, loop volume and valve sizes are engineering assumptions chosen to be consistent with that duty. Kinetics: Vanden Bussche & Froment (1996) for CO2 + 3H2 ⇌ CH3OH + H2O and CO2 + H2 ⇌ CO + H2O, with a pellet effectiveness factor; log10 K1 = 3066/T − 10.592 (bar⁻²), log10 K2 = −2073/T + 2.029. The card quotes a duty of 89 MW; the model releases about 85 MW because part of the methanol comes from CO2.

3 · Control scheme

LoopMeasuresMovesOn air failureNotes
FIC-202Make-up syngas FT-202FV-202Fail closedSets the plant rate. XV-202 (SIS) upstream.
FIC-201Converter feed FT-201C-201 speedSpeed heldCirculation = recycle + make-up.
PIC-203Loop pressure at V-201Purge PV-203Fail closedDirect acting. Purge rate = converter health signal.
LIC-204V-201 levelLV-204Fail closedDirect acting. LSHH-204 trips at 90 %.
TIC-211Bed 1 inletTV-211 (E-201 cold-side bypass)Fail openMore bypass = colder bed 1. Feed/effluent positive feedback: tune slow.
TIC-221 / 231 / 241Bed 2 / 3 / 4 inletsQuench TV-221 / 231 / 241Fail openOpening a quench valve also takes gas from bed 1.
HIC-214—E-204 steamFail closedStart-up only.

The loops interact. The quench valves share one feed: opening TV-221 cools bed 2 but starves bed 1, whose exit then rises and heats bed 2 again. The feed/effluent interchanger E-201 feeds the converter's own heat back to bed 1. When two loops fight, change one thing at a time and wait for the beds to settle.

4 · Safety systems

SIS: the make-up shut-off XV-202 opens only from IDLE with every start permissive met. A trip closes it and puts FIC-202 in MAN at 0 %; C-201 keeps running (except LSHH-204 and ESD) so the circulating gas carries heat out of the beds. With no make-up the reaction dies within minutes and the beds cool: stop C-201 early if you want a hot restart.

Alarm limits

5 · Operating rules

  1. Never above 285 °C in any bed. Cu/ZnO catalyst sinters and loses activity for good; TSHH trips at 300 °C.
  2. No make-up on cold catalyst. Below about 200 °C the catalyst does not light off; the syngas only pressurises the loop.
  3. Circulation before make-up; make-up off before circulation. Reacting gas that stops moving overheats the catalyst.
  4. Change one thing at a time and wait. A bed takes 5–15 minutes to settle; inerts take an hour. Move make-up in steps of 10 kNm³/h.
  5. Hotter is not always better. A bed near equilibrium makes less methanol when it runs hotter. Check the approach on the Converter profile before raising an inlet.
  6. Watch the purge. At a fixed make-up, a rising purge means the converter converts less per pass (ageing, poisoning, hot separator, leaks, inerts).
  7. Two instruments before you believe one: TIC-221 against FI-222 and the bed 2 profile; PIC-203 against PI-201 and the local gauge; AIT-208 against the lab.
  8. Acknowledge every alarm and say out loud what it means.

  2. Visit the five DCS displays. On the Converter profile sketch the CH3OH–temperature diagram and mark the design operating lines and quench lines.
  3. Complete the DCS reading sheet (Exercises tab). Graded out of 15.
  4. Read the Process tab and check that the three balances close at design.

Part B · What-if predictions (about 20 min)

For each event predict ↑ / ↓ / = for all eight variables 30 minutes after the event before pressing Check my predictions. Explain every wrong prediction with the equilibrium diagram or a loop balance.

    The process · methanol synthesis in a quench converter

    How the converter and its loop work, what each unit does, and the steady state they run at. Design numbers are built from the simulator's design point; the Now columns follow the running plant while this tab is open.

    Process guide · interactive slide deck (139 slides, 8 parts)
    Theory, design, operation, P&ID and control, DCS screens, other unit operations and every exercise, with live calculators built on this simulator's own model. Opens full screen inside this page; ← → to move, T for contents, Esc to close.
    1 Operating principles · 2 Block flow diagram · 3 Process description · 4 What each unit does · 5 Stream table · 6 Unit conditions · 7 Balances · 8 Key relationships

    1 · Operating principles

    ReactionHeat (at about 250 °C)MolesRole
    CO2 + 3 H2 ⇌ CH3OH + H2O−58 kJ/mol4 → 2The methanol-forming step on Cu/ZnO (it makes water)
    CO2 + H2 ⇌ CO + H2O (reverse water-gas shift)+40 kJ/mol2 → 2Fast; runs backwards here, turning CO + H2O into CO2 + H2
    Net: CO + 2 H2 ⇌ CH3OH−98 kJ/mol3 → 1Most of the heat and most of the methanol

    Equilibrium limits the conversion

    Both methanol-forming reactions release heat and lose moles. Heat means the equilibrium constant falls as the temperature rises (log10K1 = 3066/T − 10.592); fewer moles mean higher pressure helps (K is in bar⁻², so the equilibrium methanol fraction rises roughly with P²). At the converter inlet pressure of bar g and 270 °C the gas can hold only about 5 % methanol before the reverse reaction balances the forward one, and every 10 °C hotter lowers that limit further. A single adiabatic bed would heat itself until it met the equilibrium curve near 290 °C – too hot for the catalyst and too little methanol. The converter therefore stops each bed early with a cold shot and leaves the gas at only about % methanol: the conversion per pass is limited, so the unconverted gas is recycled after the methanol has been condensed out.

    Kinetics and the catalyst window

    Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 is barely active below about 200 °C and sinters (loses copper surface for good) above about 280–290 °C. The rate rises steeply with temperature (apparent activation energy roughly halved by pore diffusion in the pellets), so bed 1, which sees the richest gas, is kinetically controlled: 1 °C at its inlet moves its exit about 2 °C. The last bed runs close to equilibrium (about 8 °C approach at design): there, a hotter inlet makes less methanol. The best inlet temperature of every bed is a compromise between rate and equilibrium.

    The quench sawtooth

    On the CH3OH–temperature diagram each bed is a straight adiabatic operating line climbing towards the green equilibrium curve (about 20–25 °C per 1 % of methanol formed). The cold shot then mixes cold feed into the hot gas: the point moves down and to the left, straight towards the feed point (97 °C, 0.3 %), because the quench both cools and dilutes. That dilution is the price of the cheap single-shell design: part of the feed skips the earlier beds.

    2 · Block flow diagram

    3 · Process description

    Make-up. Fresh syngas ( kNm³/h) from the syngas compressor enters through FV-202 (FIC-202) and the SIS shut-off XV-202 and joins the recycle gas at the circulator suction. Its stoichiometric number SN = (H2 − CO2)/(CO + CO2) is about 2.9: more hydrogen than the reaction needs, which is why the loop gas is about 80 % H2 and why a purge is needed.

    Circulation and heat recovery. C-201 raises the gas from the separator pressure to about bar g at the converter inlet and circulates kNm³/h (FIC-201). The cold interchanger E-202 heats all of it to °C; the split then sends kNm³/h through the hot interchanger E-201 (bypass TV-211, TIC-211) to bed 1 at °C, and the rest as cold shots.

    Converter R-201. Four adiabatic beds hold 184 m³ of catalyst (12/20/28/40 %). Bed 1 rises from to °C; the cold shots TV-221/231/241 reset beds 2, 3 and 4 to , and °C, and they climb to , and °C. The reactions release MW; the outlet carries % methanol, close to equilibrium at the outlet temperature.

    Cooling and separation. The effluent heats the feed in E-201 and E-202 (the converter heats its own feed: feed/effluent positive feedback), is cooled to 40 °C in E-203 by cooling water, and the crude methanol (about 85 wt % methanol, the rest water) condenses in V-201 and is let down on level control (LIC-204) to distillation: t/h of crude containing t/h of methanol.

    Purge and pressure. The gas leaving V-201 is recycled except for the purge ( kNm³/h through PV-203 to reformer fuel), which PIC-203 uses to hold bar g. At a fixed make-up, anything that lowers conversion per pass raises the loop pressure, and the purge opens to carry the unconverted gas away: the purge rate is the loop's health signal.

    Start-up and shutdown. From cold, C-201 circulates the loop gas while the steam heater E-204 heats the catalyst to about 210 °C; then the SIS admits make-up, the reaction lights, the loop pressure rises to 75 bar g and E-204 is shut as E-201 takes over. For a stop, the make-up is shut, the loop circulated for about 5 minutes at half flow (at full flow the cooler would take some 80 MW out of the beds and cool them about 100 °C in 10 minutes) and C-201 stopped with the loop blocked in: the beds stay above 200 °C for a quick restart.

    Safety. The SIS closes XV-202 on a bed above 300 °C (I-1), low circulation (I-2), separator level high-high (I-3, also stopping C-201), loop pressure high-high (I-4) or the ESD button (I-5). PSV-201 protects the loop at 88 bar g; HV-205 depressures it to flare.

    5 · Differences between the sheets, the drawing above and the simulator

    • Field hand valves: the simulator's Field tab has three hand valves added after the sheets were issued — LB-204 (globe bypass round LV-204), PB-203 (globe bypass round PV-203) and BV-231 (block valve upstream of TV-231). Rev A of the sheets does not show them; they belong in rev B.
    • Trip actions: the sheet tables give "XV-202 + E-204 off" (C-201 also stops on I-3 and I-5). The simulator does the same and also puts FIC-202 in MAN at 0 %, so FV-202 is shut before XV-202 is reset — a BPCS action, not an SIS one.
    • TSHH-2xx is drawn as one SIS function on the multipoint bed thermocouples; voting is "TBC" on the sheet. The simulator trips on any single thermocouple above 300 °C for 5 s, using the same elements as the DCS indication (see the Safety layers tab's independence check).
    • FSLL-201 is drawn on the same flow element as FIC-201, as in the simulator: one transmitter for control and trip (a gap the HAZOP and LOPA tabs record).
    • ESD: the sheets name the pushbutton HS-200; the simulator's SIS tab calls it "Emergency shutdown".
    • Hardware the drawing above leaves out: line numbers and sizes, flow elements, the condensate outlet of E-204, the demister and level gauge of V-201, off-sheet connectors and design notes.

        Design of the unit operation · R-201 methanol converter and synthesis loop

        Teaching slide deck · Design of the unit operation — equilibrium and kinetics, adiabatic rise and quench, loop balances, interchangers, operating conditions and conceptual sizing of a quench converter loop.
        Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

        How a quench-converter synthesis loop like R-201 is specified and roughed out before detailed design. Every number on this page is taken from the simulator at its design point ( t/h methanol, loop bar g) when the page opens. The sizing in part 5 is conceptual: rules of thumb and simple correlations, not a licensor's reactor design.

        1 Fundamentals and principle · 2 Components · 3 Setting the operating conditions · 4 Conceptual design · 5 Conceptual sizing (calculator)

        1 · Fundamentals and principle of the unit operation

        Methanol is made from synthesis gas (H₂, CO, CO₂) over a Cu/ZnO/Al₂O₃ catalyst at 220–280 °C and 50–100 bar. Only a few per cent of the gas turns into methanol in one pass, because equilibrium limits it and the reactions release heat that the catalyst cannot tolerate. So the plant is built as a loop: the converter makes a little methanol, the effluent is cooled so the methanol condenses, and the unconverted gas is recycled by a circulator. The quench converter R-201 handles the heat by splitting the catalyst into four adiabatic beds and injecting cold feed gas between them.

        1.1 The reactions and their equilibrium

        (1) CO₂ + 3 H₂ ⇌ CH₃OH + H₂O   ΔH = −58 kJ/mol
        (2) CO₂ + H₂ ⇌ CO + H₂O   ΔH = +40 kJ/mol (reverse water-gas shift)
        Net for CO: (1) − (2) gives CO + 2 H₂ ⇌ CH₃OH, ΔH ≈ −98 kJ/mol.

        Both methanol reactions lose two moles of gas for each mole of methanol, so high pressure favours methanol; they are exothermic, so low temperature favours it. The equilibrium constants in the simulator (assumed, Workbook) are log₁₀ K₁ = 3066/T − 10.592 (bar⁻²) and log₁₀ K₂ = −2073/T + 2.029. At the bed-1 inlet (220 °C) K₁ = bar⁻² and K₂ = . Going from 240 to 260 °C cuts K₁ by %, while K₂ rises.

        Equilibrium methanol at each bed-exit temperature and pressure, for the converter feed composition, compared with what the beds actually reach:

        Bed 1Bed 2Bed 3Bed 4
        Bed exit temperature (°C)
        Equilibrium CH₃OH at that exit (mol %)
        Actual CH₃OH at the exit (mol %)
        Temperature at which the actual gas would be at equilibrium (°C)
        Approach to equilibrium ΔTapp (K)

        The approach to equilibrium is the distance, in kelvin, between the bed exit and the temperature at which the exit gas would be in equilibrium. Bed 1 is far from equilibrium ( K: kinetics limit it); bed 4 ends only K away. A larger last bed or more catalyst would add little: to make more methanol per pass the gas must be cooled and brought back — which is what the loop does.

        1.2 Kinetics and the effectiveness factor

        The simulator uses the Vanden Bussche–Froment (1996) rate expressions: methanol forms from CO₂, the rate is proportional to pCO₂pH₂(1 − approach term), and water strongly inhibits it. At the bed-1 inlet the intrinsic rates are r₁ = and r₂ = mmol per kg catalyst per second.

        The catalyst pellets are several millimetres across, so H₂ and CO₂ cannot reach the pellet centre as fast as they react. The effectiveness factor η = tanh φ / φ (Thiele modulus φ) is the fraction of the pellet that works. In the model η = at 220 / 240 / 260 / 280 °C: the hotter the catalyst, the faster the reaction and the thinner the working shell, so internal diffusion halves the apparent activation energy. Bed inlets η = . With an activity factor of for bed 1, the effective rate at its inlet is mmol/(kg s).

        1.3 Heat of reaction and the adiabatic temperature rise

        At design the converter makes kmol/h of methanol. Reaction (1) runs forward and releases MW; reaction (2) runs backwards (CO is consumed, kmol/h) and releases a further MW. Together this is MW, i.e. kJ per mol of methanol for this gas.

        An adiabatic bed keeps all this heat in the gas. With a mean heat capacity of kJ/(kmol K):

        ΔTad per mol % of methanol made = 0.01 × ΔH / cp = 0.01 × × 1000 / ≈ K per %

        The four beds rise K while methanol rises mol %, i.e. K per % (lower than the simple figure because the moles shrink and the quench gas dilutes the bed gas). If one bed had to make all of it ( → % with no quench) the gas would heat up by about K, far past the catalyst limit — hence several beds with cooling between them.

        1.4 Quench mixing: why each bed inlet drops

        Between beds, cold feed gas at °C (after E-202, TI-203) is injected through a lozenge distributor. The inlet temperature of the next bed follows from an enthalpy balance on the mixing zone:

        Tin,n = (Gn−1 cp Tex,n−1 + qn cp Tq) / ((Gn−1 + qn) cp)    so    qn / Gn−1 = (Tex,n−1 − Tin,n) / (Tin,n − Tq)

        Bed 2: kNm³/h leave bed 1 at °C and kNm³/h of quench join them: T = °C, the set point of TIC-221 ( °C). The quench needed per unit of upstream gas is % for beds 2 / 3 / 4. The feed therefore splits % between bed 1 and the three cold shots (FI-212 / 222 / 232 / 242 = kNm³/h). Two consequences: each quench dilutes the methanol already made, and it increases the flow through every bed below it.

        1.5 Recycle ratio and the loop balances

        • Recycle ratio R/M = ( − ) / = . The converter sees about five times the make-up flow; per pass only % of the CO + CO₂ in the converter feed is converted.
        • Stoichiometric number SN = (H₂ − CO₂)/(CO + CO₂). Methanol needs SN = 2. The make-up (H₂ , CO , CO₂ %) has SN = : steam-reformed gas carries surplus hydrogen. The surplus accumulates, so the loop gas is H₂-rich ( % H₂ in V-201 gas, SN ≈ ) and the converter feed has SN = . The purge must remove it: kNm³/h of H₂ go to fuel.
        • Carbon efficiency = carbon to methanol / carbon in make-up (CO + CO₂ + CH₄) = / kmol/h = %. The rest leaves in the purge ( kmol/h as CO, CO₂ and CH₄ plus kmol/h as methanol vapour).
        • Inert balance fixes the purge. CH₄ and N₂ do not react and leave only with the purge: M yinert,MU = Pu yinert,loop. With % inerts in the make-up and % in the loop gas, Pu = × / = kNm³/h (FI-203). CH₄ in = , CH₄ out = kNm³/h. Less purge means more inerts in the loop, lower reactant partial pressures and less methanol per pass; more purge wastes carbon and hydrogen.
        • Methanol left in the gas. V-201 at °C: yMeOH ≈ xMeOH psat / P = % (crude xMeOH = ). This methanol returns to the converter and some leaves with the purge.

        1.6 Feed–effluent interchangers E-201 and E-202, cooler E-203 and circulator C-201

        • E-202 (cold interchanger) heats all the converter feed from °C (C-201 discharge) to °C with effluent that has already passed E-201: MW, ΔTLM K, UA ≈ kW/K. Its cold outlet is also the quench-gas temperature.
        • E-201 (hot interchanger) heats the bed-1 feed to °C with the converter effluent ( → °C): MW, ΔTLM K, UA ≈ kW/K. About % of the bed-1 feed bypasses its cold side through TV-211 ( % open), which is how TIC-211 trims the bed-1 inlet to 220 °C. This is a positive feedback: a hotter converter heats its own feed more. Without the bypass margin the loop could run away; with it the temperature is controllable.
        • E-203 (water cooler) takes the effluent from to °C. The simulator counts only the sensible heat, MW, giving the CW return of °C with about t/h of cooling water. In a real cooler the condensing crude adds about MW more (assumed latent heats), and E-202 already starts condensing.
        • C-201 only has to overcome the loop pressure drop, bar: pressure ratio , temperature rise K, MW ( kW per kNm³/h). Circulation costs power, so pressure drop through the beds ( bar, PDI-215…245) and exchangers is a design variable.

        3 · Setting the operating conditions (การกำหนดสภาวะในการทำงาน)

        The loop has nine independent handles (see the Control loop design tab). Each operating condition is chosen from a process reason and then checked against an equipment or catalyst limit. Limits below are read from the page's alarm table and SIS trip settings.

        Order in which the conditions are set

        1. Pressure and circulation first. Pressurise the loop with gas and start C-201; the SIS will not admit make-up below % circulation, because circulating gas is what carries the heat out of the beds.
        2. Heat the catalyst with E-204 until bed 1 is above °C: below that the copper catalyst is too slow to start.
        3. Admit make-up slowly in MAN. As bed 1 lights off, the effluent gets hotter and E-201 takes over the heating from E-204; TIC-211 then trims the bed-1 inlet.
        4. Bring in the quenches (TIC-221/231/241 in AUTO) as each bed starts to rise, then put PIC-203 (purge) and LIC-204 (let-down) in AUTO.
        5. Raise make-up to rate and adjust circulation so that bed exits stay below their alarms.
        6. Optimise: bed inlets as low as the catalyst activity allows (more equilibrium methanol, cooler exits), inerts and purge at the economic balance, separator as cold as the cooling water allows.

        Operating window

        Minimum: circulation must stay above the FSLL-201 trip ( % = kNm³/h), and the bed inlets above the light-off temperature. Cutting circulation at full make-up overheats the beds: at 1 400 kNm³/h the hottest catalyst reaches °C, above the °C trip. Maximum: heat removal and catalyst temperature, not the converter volume. Make-up 400 kNm³/h gives t/h with a hottest bed at °C; 450 kNm³/h gives t/h but °C, over the °C bed-exit alarm. More circulation cools the beds but costs power and C-201 runs out of speed near kNm³/h (speed %). Low make-up (300 kNm³/h) gives t/h. Aged catalyst (−60 % activity) makes only t/h at design make-up and the purge rises to kNm³/h. (Runs of the simulator model, 50 min each.)

        4.2 Design decisions

Penalty: quench dilutes the product, so outlet CH₃OH is lower (≈ 5 %) and circulation higher than in steam-raising designs (≈ 7–8 %), and no HP steam is raised.
        Number of beds2 … 64Adiabatic rise ≈ K per % methanol; limiting each bed to about 40–55 K needs at least three beds for ≈ 4.5 % made; the fourth gives margin and better approach to equilibrium.
        Catalyst splitEqual · increasing12 / 20 / 28 / 40 %Bed 1 sees the most reactive gas (far from equilibrium) and must stay short to limit its exit temperature; later beds react slower and need more catalyst.
        Pressure50–100 bar75–80 barHigher pressure raises equilibrium and rate (smaller loop) but costs syngas compression and a thicker shell; 50–100 bar is usual for modern Cu catalysts.

        Feed–effluent heat interchangeOne exchanger · two in series · steam raisingE-201 (hot) + E-202 (cold); E-204 steam for start-upRecovers the reaction heat to preheat the feed (the reaction then sustains itself); E-202 gives cold quench gas. The bypass TV-211 controls the positive feedback.
        PurgeTo reformer fuel · to H₂ recovery (PSA/membrane) · flareReformer fuelUses the heating value of the H₂ and CH₄; H₂ recovery would raise carbon efficiency where the SN surplus is large (SN = ).
        Control philosophyPressure by purge or by make-up; bed inlets by quench or by interbed exchangersMake-up on flow (plant rate), pressure by purge (PIC-203), circulation by speed, bed inlets by quench and bypassThe front end sets the rate; the purge is the natural outlet for surplus gas; quench valves act within seconds on each bed.
        Safety (SIS)Single or redundant shut-off; which tripsXV-202 make-up shut-off on high bed temperature, low circulation, high separator level, high pressure, ESD; PSV-201; HV-205 blowdownStopping the fresh gas stops the heat source. Gaps (shared transmitters, single thermocouples, single valve) are listed in the HAZOP and Safety layers tabs.

        4.3 Design sequence

        1. Production and make-up: methanol rate → carbon efficiency → make-up flow; SN of the make-up (part 5 step 1).
        2. Inert balance → purge flow; choose the inert level in the loop (step 2).
        3. Separator conditions → methanol and water in crude, methanol left in the loop gas (step 3).
        4. Choose converter outlet CH₃OH (equilibrium and catalyst volume) → circulation and recycle ratio (step 4).
        5. Heat of reaction and adiabatic rise → number of beds (step 5).
        6. Catalyst volume from GHSV and its split; bed inlet/exit temperatures → quench fractions (steps 6–7).
        7. Vessel diameter from pressure drop (Ergun) → bed heights and vessel height (step 8).
        8. Circulator, interchangers and cooler duties (steps 9–11); then kinetic rating of the beds, mechanical design, control and SIS.

        5 · Conceptual sizing

        Change any input; results update immediately. Defaults reproduce R-201 and its loop (read from the simulator when the page opens). The column "R-201 loop (simulator)" shows the lined-out simulator values. Checks marked ✗ are outside the usual guideline or the page's alarms.

        Production and make-up
        Loop and converter
        Beds and quench
        Vessel (Ergun)
        Circulator and exchangers

        Assumptions and limits of this sizing

        • Gas heat capacity per kmol is constant through the converter; the hot-side heat-capacity flow is corrected for the moles lost and the component cp change per kmol methanol made (model value).
        • Carbon efficiency, inert level and outlet CH₃OH are inputs; in a real design they come out of a loop simulation with the kinetics. Default values are the simulator's.
        • Crude water from an oxygen balance; the CO₂ share of the carbon oxides in the purge is taken from the loop gas. Methanol in V-201 vapour by Raoult's law (ideal liquid).
        • Quench fractions from the mixing balances with the bed inlet and exit temperatures as design targets; the heat released by the beds is checked against the heat of reaction (they differ by the mole shrinkage and cp change, about 2 %).
        • Catalyst volume from GHSV on the converter feed (design card range 8 000–12 000 h⁻¹); bulk density is the simulator's catalyst mass over 184 m³. Minimum bed count = adiabatic rise / allowed rise, a rough screen only.
        • Diameter from the Ergun equation on bed 4 (all the gas) with assumed particle size, voidage and viscosity; distributor and grid losses are not included (the simulator's bed ΔP readings include them). Quench-zone and end allowances are assumed.
        • C-201: ideal gas, polytropic temperature rise with (k − 1)/k and efficiency as in the model. E-203: sensible duty as in the simulator plus a condensing duty from assumed latent heats. Guidelines quoted are typical practice, not a licensor's design rules.

        2 · The block flow diagram

        Make-up syngas (1) joins the recycle gas (2) at the circulator suction. The converter feed (3) is heated in E-202 (4); most of it goes on through E-201 and E-204 to bed 1 (5), the rest is the cold shot to beds 2–4 (6). The effluent (7) gives its heat back in E-201 (8) and E-202 (9), is cooled in E-203 and separated in V-201: vapour (10) recycles, a small part leaves as purge (11), and the condensed crude methanol (12) leaves to let-down. The purge and the crude are the only exits.

        3 · What goes in and out of each block

        4 · Stream table (design and now)

        From the Process tab's streamsOf(). Gas flows in kNm³/h, crude methanol in t/h; composition H₂ / CO / CO₂ / CH₃OH / inerts (CH₄ + N₂) in mol %.

        5 · Boundary balances

        Draw a boundary round a block and count what crosses it. The first three rows are computed from the model's states (Process tab part 7). The exchanger rows are also computed the way the DCS would do it, flow × cp × ΔT from measured values, so the two ways can be compared. A row turns red only when its difference moves more than 2 points from its value at design.

        6 · From BFD to PFD

        • Each block becomes equipment with a tag: "Front end" stays a battery-limit arrow, "C-201" becomes the circulator with its suction mixing point, "R-201" gets its four beds and the three quench valves TV-221/231/241, "V-201" gets its level valve LV-204 and the purge valve PV-203.
        • Streams get their own PFD numbers and flags with flow, temperature and pressure where the model gives them; on PFD-201 numbers 1–12 are the same as the BFD, and the extra internal lines are numbered from 13 on.
        • Control valves on the main streams appear (FV-202, TV-211, the quench valves, PV-203, LV-204) together with the blowdown HV-205; instruments, trips and manual valves wait for the P&ID.
        • Utilities (cooling water to E-203, HP steam to E-204) are drawn where they enter, not as blocks.

        PFD · Process flow diagram PFD-201 (R-201 synthesis loop)

        PFD-201 was drawn to ISO 10628 conventions with Turton stream numbers and information flags, signed by the drawer in the title block. Flags carry numbers only where the simulator gives them; this page sets each flag beside the model value, design and now. The same drawing carries the study areas on the HAZID tab.

        1 What a PFD adds · 2 The drawing · 3 Equipment list · 4 Flags and the model · 5 Reading the PFD · 6 What the P&ID adds

        1 · What a PFD adds to the BFD

        • Equipment instead of blocks: every major item with its tag and a symbol in proportion to the real item (R-201 drawn 24 m tall and 5 m wide, the interchangers as shell-and-tube units, V-201 with its demister).
        • Stream numbers with flags (gas flow, mass flow, temperature, pressure) where the heat and mass balance gives them. Numbers 1–12 are the BFD numbers; internal lines that only carry a split or a mix are numbered from 13 and have no flag.
        • The main control valves: FV-202 make-up, TV-211 bypass, the quench valves TV-221/231/241, PV-203 purge, LV-204 let-down, and the blowdown HV-205 to flare.
        • Utilities where they enter: HP steam to E-204, cooling water to E-203.

        2 · The drawing

        PDF (A4)PowerPoint (editable)SVGPNG

        The PowerPoint file opens from the zip or GitHub Pages copy; claude.ai serves the PDF, SVG and PNG.

        3 · Equipment list

        4 · Flags beside the model

        Drawing = the number printed in the flag; Design = the simulator's design state (noise off); Now = the running simulator. ✓ means the flag agrees with the model within 3 %.

        5 · Reading the PFD

        • Two fluids are never mixed except where the process mixes them: the cold shots join the converter gas on purpose; in E-201 and E-202 feed and effluent are on opposite sides of the tubes, and cooling water and steam never meet the process gas.
        • What goes in comes out: make-up (1) leaves as purge (11) and crude methanol (12); check it on the BFD tab's boundary balances.
        • Pressure falls along each path: about 86 bar g at the make-up battery limit → 80.6 bar g at the C-201 discharge → 79.7 bar g at the converter inlet → about 75 bar g in V-201, where C-201 lifts it again. The make-up must enter above the loop pressure, which is why FV-202 needs the front end's pressure margin.
        • One recycle: V-201 vapour (10) returns to C-201 as stream 2 about four times larger than the make-up; the purge (11) is the only way out for CH₄ and N₂.
        • Heat recovery loop: the effluent (7) heats the feed twice (E-201 then E-202) before the cooler; the hotter the effluent, the hotter the feed — a positive feedback the TV-211 bypass controls.

        6 · What the P&ID adds

        • Every instrument and loop (FIC-201 on the circulator speed, FIC-202, PIC-203, LIC-204, TIC-211 and TIC-221/231/241, HIC-214), the trips (TSHH on the bed thermocouples, FSLL-201, LSHH-204, PSHH-203, ESD) and their final element XV-202.
        • Fail positions (quench and bypass valves fail open, make-up, purge and let-down valves fail closed), manual block valves, check valves, drains and vents, line numbers and sizes.
        • Relief: PSV-201 at 88 bar g to flare, and the blowdown HV-205.
        • See the P&ID tab: the screen drawing used by the DCS console, and the EPC sheets MEOH-PID-001 and MEOH-PID-002 below it.

        Operating windows · where the R-201 loop can run, what limits it, and how much room there is

        Teaching slide deck · Operating windows — operability, variability, bounds and the integrity operating window, capacity and turndown, and the Type I, II and III windows worked on the R-201 methanol loop model.
        Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

        Follows the course lecture Operating Windows (2105625 Process Analysis and Improvement, after T. Marlin's Process Operability class materials). Every window on this tab was computed on copies of this simulator's own model: Type I runs and Type II/III runs, each run 3000 s to steady state with the trips switched off, so the limits can be seen rather than cut short. The live plant is never touched. Limits come from the page's alarms (ALM), trips (K.trip*) and valve ranges; limits marked "assumed" are for teaching.

        1 Operability · 2 Variability · 3 Bounds and IOW · 4 Worst case and point check · 5 Capacity and turndown · 6 Type I window · 7 Type II and III window · 8 Monte Carlo window · 9 Manipulated variables · 10 Holes and limitations

        1 · Operability and the operating window

        Process operability means the plant has the capacity and flexibility to reach a range of operating conditions safely, reliably, profitably, with good dynamic performance and product quality. The operating window is the range of achievable steady-state operation: the set of conditions for which every controlled variable can be held at its set point and no limit is broken. Four things shape it.

        The variables of the R-201 loop

        ClassVariable (tag)DesignWhy it is in this class

        2 · Variability: the design basis the window must cover

        "The abnormal is normal." A window is only as good as the list of changes it was sized for. The lecture's five sources of variability, written as a design-basis memorandum for the loop. Ranges are the ones the model can represent (its fault severities); frequencies are teaching values.

        SourceWhat changes in the loopRange used hereHow oftenCovered by

        A single human error must not cause an unsafe condition and must not stay undetected. That is why the bounds in part 3 have alarms and, where damage is fast (catalyst runaway, overpressure, liquid to the circulator), trips.

        3 · Bounds and the integrity operating window

        The bounds are the frame of the window: upper and lower limits set by materials, design parameters and performance. A hard bound must not be crossed: the TSHH trip temperature, PSHH-203 and the PSV set pressure, the low-circulation trip. A soft bound can be crossed for a while, but something degrades: the Cu catalyst sinters above about 285 °C, inerts build up, methanol is recycled from a warm separator. Capacity bounds are the ends of a handle's travel: a valve at 5 % or 95 % can no longer hold its variable. The table gives the design value, the live value and the margin to each limit.

        BoundKindWhy it existsLimitDesignNowMargin now ÷ margin at design

        Reading the IOW (API RP 584). Inside the target range the loop is stable and the catalyst lasts. Between the target range and the standard limit (the alarm) it is still safe, but time counts: sintering, inert build-up and methanol recycle accumulate. Past the critical limit failure is quick; that is where the trips of the Safety layers tab act. On this loop the hard bounds are about runaway and containment (bed temperature, pressure, circulation, separator level), and the soft bounds about catalyst life and efficiency.

        Target ranges and the limits marked "assumed" are teaching values; the others are the page's alarms and trips.

        4 · Design for the worst case, and a live point check

        Equipment is sized for the worst case of the variability it must handle. For a heat exchanger (Q = U A ΔTlm) the worst case is the highest duty at the smallest temperature difference with the most fouling. In the loop each piece of equipment has its own worst case. Pick one, or set your own point: the page runs this model to steady state (every controller in AUTO at the set points below, trips off) and checks every bound.

        5 · Capacity and turndown

        A small plant that only just meets the design point is cheap but has no window; a large one has a window but costs capital and runs inefficiently at low rate. The lecture's rule: the capacity must be safe, protect expensive equipment and meet quality for the base case and frequently occurring variability; lower production is acceptable in rare cases; stop for extreme ones. Turndown ratio = normal maximum ÷ normal minimum, where "normal" means sustainable without hazard or damage.

        Each element of the loop allows its own range of make-up gas. The loop's range is the overlap, so it is always narrower than any single element's. Ranges below are at fresh catalyst, 32 °C cooling water, normal gas and the design set points (circulation kNm³/h, loop bar g), interpolated in the Type III column of part 7.

        ElementTurndown or rangeability in this loopTypical (lecture)Flexibility class

        6 · Steady-state operating window, Type I: what the throughput handles can reach

        The lecture writes the model as y = A u + B d + C (y controlled variables, u manipulated, d disturbances) and poses three problems:

        TypeGivenFindIn the R-201 loop

        An honest label. The loop has two throughput handles: the make-up gas (FIC-202 → FV-202) and the circulation (FIC-201 → C-201 speed). In the strict Type I problem the raw valves move and everything else is fixed. Here the two flow set points stand in for FV-202 and the C-201 speed, while the pressure, level and four bed-inlet loops stay in AUTO, so each cell is a closed-loop steady state: the question answered is "which make-up and circulation pairs can the loop hold with its own controllers doing the rest". Make-up enters as a disturbance for the loop in Type II/III (it is set by the front end), but it is a handle here.

        outlined cells = every bound met · ring = design

        7 · Type II and Type III: the disturbances the loop can absorb

        Now the controlled variables sit at their design set points (circulation, loop pressure, four bed inlets, level) while the disturbances move: the make-up rate from the front end, and the catalyst activity as it ages over its 3–4 year run. Type II reads the handle positions each disturbance needs; Type III keeps only the points where every handle is inside its range and every bound holds, and colours the rest by the bound that fails first (capacity and hard bounds before "set point not held").

        8 · Monte Carlo operating window

        The lecture's recipe: (1) simulate the base case, (2) replace the uncertain inputs by samples from their distributions and repeat, (3) mark each sample feasible or infeasible against every bound, (4) report the fraction and show it graphically. Here the make-up rate is normal, the cooling-water temperature uniform, and the catalyst activity uniform inside a band (a year of the run). Each sample's margin is interpolated in the Type III grids of part 7 (make-up × ageing, at 32 and 38 °C), for the make-up gas chosen above.

        9 · Manipulated variables: enough, strong, independent, fast

        With n adjustable handles and m variables to hold: n = m gives a finite window with each point exactly specified; n < m gives no window (at best the design point) and is not an acceptable design; n > m leaves extra freedom (several ways to reach a point, which can be used to optimise).

        Held variable (m)Handle (n)Steady-state effect of the handle (+5 % output, every loop in manual except the level)
        Lecture criterionCheck on the R-201 loop

          Flexibility · the handles that steer the R-201 loop through its operating window

          Teaching slide deck · Flexibility — how many handles, where they act, flexibility for gas flow, heat transfer and production rate, and the end-of-run choices as the catalyst ages, worked on the R-201 methanol loop model.
          Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

          Follows the course lecture Flexibility (2105625 Process Analysis and Improvement, after T. Marlin's Process Operability class materials). The Operating windows tab finds where the loop can run; this tab looks at the handles that move it there. Gains, capacities and strategy results come from runs on copies of this simulator's model ( steady-state runs, trips off) or from the model's own equations, which are quoted where they are used.

          1 What flexibility is · 2 How many · 3 Where · 4 Gas and liquid flow · 5 Heat transfer · 6 Production rate · 7 End of run · 8 How much · 9 Recommendations

          1 · What flexibility is

          Flexibility is the ability of a plant to operate reliably across a wide range of rates and conditions without losing quantity or quality. Some controlled variables are held at their set points while disturbances arrive; flexibility is what lets us steer the process after the equipment has been built.

          Without flexibility the loop passes every disturbance on: a richer make-up gas would go straight into bed temperatures, an aged catalyst straight into lost production. With flexibility the quench and bypass valves hold the bed inlets, the purge holds the pressure, and the circulator and set points recover some of what ageing takes.

          How it is provided

          • Spare capacity in the circulator (speed), valves, exchangers and the catalyst volume itself.
          • Adjustable utility flows: cooling water to E-203, steam to E-204.
          • By-passes: TV-211 around the E-201 cold side, the quench (cold-shot) lines around beds 1–3, PB-203 and LB-204 around the purge and let-down valves.

          Four design questions: how many handles, where, which tools (valves, speed, by-passes), and how much capacity.

          The flexibility register of the R-201 loop

          HandleWhat it adjustsKind of flexibilityAt designSpare at designStatus

          2 · How many handles? Degrees of freedom

          A successful design needs number of adjustable valves ≥ number of variables to be held. The maximum number of controlled variables equals the degrees of freedom, and the minimum number of handles equals the number of variables we insist on.

          Variable the loop must holdWhyHandle used

          3 · Where? Causal paths from each handle

          Each held variable needs a handle with an independent causal path to it. Interaction is allowed as long as every desired point can still be reached. The lecture's three cases:

          Steady-state effect of +5 % on each handle, every loop in manual except the level (LIC-204 stays in AUTO because the level integrates), 6000 s on the model. These are the numbers behind the causal map; bold cells are the large effects.

          Interaction without dependence: a 2 × 2 inverse

          Pick a pair. Ask for a change in the two held variables and the page solves the 2 × 2 steady-state gain model for the two valve moves, with the relative gain λ₁₁ of the pairing shown.

          4 · Flexibility for gas and liquid flow

          For a gas loop the flow settles where the machine's head equals the losses of the loop: circulator, E-202, E-201, four catalyst beds, E-203 and V-201 in series. Only the circulator speed is adjustable in that path. The flows that enter and leave the loop (make-up, purge, crude) each pass one control valve, and the pressure difference across that valve sets its capacity.

          4a · Circulation: C-201 speed (the model's own relation)

          Model relation: F = (speed/100) · · (1 − loss) · Psep,abs/ (volumetric machine, flow ∝ speed × gas density). The model has no surge line; a real centrifugal circulator also needs an anti-surge recycle at low flow.

          4b · Make-up: FV-202 against the loop pressure (the model's own equation)

          M = Km · x · √(Pmu − Ploop) with Km = kmol/s per √bar (FV-202 linear). The valve works on only about 11 bar of difference, so the loop pressure matters: every bar the loop rises takes away a share of the valve's capacity, and the syngas compressor discharge pressure is the real ceiling. The supply-pressure range on the slider is assumed.

          4c · Purge and let-down: the two inventory valves

          5 · Flexibility for heat transfer

          Q = U A ΔT*: flexibility can act on U (a flow changes the film coefficient), on A (active area), or on ΔT (a utility's temperature or flow, a by-pass that mixes). In a quench converter the biggest "exchanger" is direct mixing: cold shot gas is added between the beds.

          Heat duty in the loopDesign dutyUAΔT*Handle today

          5a · E-201 and its TV-211 by-pass: how much fouling can the by-pass absorb?

          The lecture's by-pass case (b): E-201's cold side is fixed by the converter feed, so part of it is sent around the exchanger and mixed back. More by-pass means less heating, so TIC-211 opens TV-211 when the converter runs hot and closes it when heat is short. Fouling lowers U: the bed 1 inlet can be held until TV-211 reaches its closed end. Model runs with E-201 UA lowered in steps (TIC-211 in AUTO):

          5b · E-203: cooling water as a utility flow (the model's own relation)

          Model relation: Tsep = Tcw + (TE-202 hot out − Tcw) · exp(−NTU · fcw0.7 · (F/Fdes)−0.3), NTU = , with the E-202 hot outlet at its design °C. Flows above 100 % assume spare pump and tower capacity.

          6 · Flexibility for production rate

          At steady state material must balance in every unit and the whole plant (no long-term accumulation). One flexible variable sets the rate; every other flow follows automatically without people, and measured flows are never simply matched to each other (meter errors would accumulate). Level and pressure show inventory: pressure for the gas in the loop, level for the crude in V-201.

          Guiding principleR-201 loop

          7 · Flexibility at end of run: what to move as the catalyst ages

          A Cu/ZnO/Al₂O₃ charge loses activity steadily over its 3–4 year run (Cu crystallites sinter). The make-up the front end sends does not fall, so the loop must convert the same gas with a weaker catalyst. There are three handles for that, each with a cost. The page ran each strategy on the model at two catalyst ages, make-up at its design kNm³/h, every loop in AUTO:

          Catalyst ageing

          8 · How much capacity? Spare room on each handle

          Move the make-up rate and the catalyst age: the bars show how far each handle must travel to hold the design set points (Type II runs of the Operating windows tab, interpolated). The first bar to reach its end sets the edge of the window.

          9 · Recommendations to widen the loop's flexibility

          HAZID · Hazard Identification of the R-201 methanol converter and synthesis loop

          Teaching slide deck · HAZID — what HAZID is, the PFD-201 study areas, the guideword checklist, catalyst and hydrogen hazards, the risk matrix, the major accident hazards and the studies that follow.
          Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

          A plant-level, checklist-driven identification of the major hazards of Methanol Converter Ver 1, done before (and wider than) the detailed HAZOP. It uses the same example risk matrix as the HAZOP and Safety layers tabs; a real study uses the owner's matrix and a multidisciplinary team. Design numbers on this page are read from the simulator's design state when the page loads.

          1 What HAZID is · 2 Method · 3 PFD and study areas · 4 Guideword checklist · 5 Hazard register · 6 Major accident hazards · 7 From HAZID to HAZOP

          1 · What HAZID is and where it sits

          HAZID (Hazard Identification) is a structured brainstorm of what could go badly wrong across the whole facility, including its surroundings, people and environment. It is done early (concept and front-end design) with the PFD, the plot plan and the design basis, so that major hazards shape the design before details are fixed. It asks broad questions ("what hazards exist in the converter area?"); the HAZOP asks detailed ones ("what if there is no flow through TV-221?").

          HAZIDHAZOP
          WhenConcept / FEED, and before major changes (e.g. a catalyst change-out campaign, a capacity increase)Detailed design with the P&ID frozen; revalidation
          DrawingPFD-201 (below), plot planP&ID tab, cause-and-effect (SIS) chart
          BreakdownAreas / systems (7 here)Nodes with one design intent (9 in the HAZOP tab)
          PromptGuideword checklist by hazard category (natural, external, inventory, pressure and temperature, reaction and catalyst, utilities, ignition, health, occupational, environment, operations, people)Guide word × parameter (NO flow, MORE temperature …)
          ScopeProcess and non-process hazards, site and surroundings, maintenance such as catalyst change-outProcess deviations and operability
          OutputHazard register, list of major accident hazards, studies to do next (HAZOP, fire and explosion, SIL, materials/HTHA review, layout)Worksheets and recommendations per deviation
          ReferenceISO 17776 (major accident hazard management in design; HAZID and its checklist); company HSE practiceIEC 61882

          2 · Method

          1. Define scope and basis: the synthesis loop from the make-up gas boundary (FV-202 / XV-202) to the let-down drum, purge-to-fuel and flare battery limits, plus the utilities it needs (steam to E-204, cooling water to E-203, instrument air, nitrogen, power) and catalyst handling; site conditions; risk matrix.
          2. Divide the plant into areas on the PFD (section 3).
          3. Apply the guideword checklist to each area (section 4): for every category ask whether the hazard exists here, what could release it (cause / threat) and what would follow (top event and outcome).
          4. Record existing controls, split into prevention (stops the top event) and mitigation (limits the outcome), as in a bow-tie.
          5. Rank the risk (S × L with the controls, same matrix as the HAZOP) and flag major accident hazards (MAH): events that could cause multiple fatalities, major damage or a major environmental release.
          6. Assign actions and further studies: design changes (the agreed additions below), HAZOP nodes, fire and explosion analysis, SIL assessment, materials and HTHA review, layout.

          3 · Process flow diagram and study areas

          PFD-201 drawn to ISO 10628 conventions. Streams 1–12 carry flow, temperature and pressure flags taken from the Process tab stream table at the design point; the other stream numbers carry no data. The coloured markers are the HAZID areas, coloured by the highest risk found there; click one to filter the register.

          PFD-201 PDF (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)Marker colour: Low Medium High Very high

          4 · Guideword checklist

          5 · Hazard register

          S and L use the risk matrix of the HAZOP tab (section 5): S 1–5 (worst credible outcome), L 1–5 with the existing controls (1 < 10⁻⁴ /y … 5 > 0.1 /y), R = S × L, 1–4 Low, 5–9 Medium, 10–16 High, 20–25 Very high. Values marked "typical practice" or "assumed" are not from the simulator.

          6 · Major accident hazards and what they lead to

            Agreed recommended additions (same names in HAZOP, Safety layers and LOPA)

            7 · From HAZID to HAZOP and other studies

            • Every process MAH is examined in detail in the HAZOP tab: gas blow-by → node N7 (V-201 and LV-204); loop overpressure → N8 (purge, blowdown, PSV-201) and N1 (make-up); bed runaway → N5 (beds and quench), N1 (make-up composition) and N2 (circulation); loss of containment of hot gas → N3 (E-201/E-202) and N5; start-up, catalyst reduction and restart → N9 (procedures).
            • Trips that protect against MAHs (TSHH I-1, FSLL-201 I-2, LSHH-204 I-3, PSHH-203 I-4) and the proposed LSLL-204 / XV-204 go to a SIL assessment (IEC 61511) in the Safety layers and LOPA tabs.
            • Fire hazards (jet fire from hot H₂, methanol pool fire, external fire) go to a fire and explosion analysis: flame and gas detection coverage (hydrogen and methanol flames are nearly invisible), depressuring time of HV-205, fireproofing and spacing.
            • Hydrogen service goes to a materials review: API 941 (Nelson curves) for HTHA at the trip temperature, PWHT, inspection.
            • Catalyst handling, confined-space entry under nitrogen, carbonyls and dust go to the maintenance procedures (permit to work, inert entry, passivation) and the PPE plan.
            • The register is revisited under management of change: a new catalyst, a higher make-up rate, or a change to the SIS.

            4 · Degrees of freedom (DOF)

            Why it matters. The degrees of freedom tell how many variables can be held at chosen values. Try to control more CVs than there are independent MVs and controllers fight over one valve; control fewer and some variable drifts wherever the disturbances push it.

            NDOF = Nvariables − Nindependent equations    and    NDOF = Ndisturbances (fixed by surroundings) + Nmanipulated

            For control the useful count is the control DOF = number of independent manipulated variables: the valves and speeds the controllers can move.

            4.1 DOF of the synthesis loop (steady state)

            Variables (22)Equations (13)
            Process (13): M make-up · F circulation · Pu purge · L crude let-down · P loop pressure · h V-201 level · y loop inerts · G methanol made · T₁ T₂ T₃ T₄ bed inlets · Qh E-204 duty
            Handles (9): FV-202 · C-201 speed · PV-203 · LV-204 · TV-211 · TV-221 · TV-231 · TV-241 · E-204 steam valve            		 1 FV-202: M = f(FV-202, Psyngas − P)
            2 C-201 curve: F = f(speed, P, ΔPloop)
            3 PV-203: Pu = f(PV-203, P)
            4 LV-204: L = f(LV-204, P, h)

            DOF = 22 − 13 = 9, exactly the nine independent handles moved by the model: FV-202, C-201 speed, PV-203, LV-204, TV-211, TV-221, TV-231, TV-241 and the E-204 steam valve. Syngas supply pressure and composition, cooling-water temperature and catalyst activity are disturbances, not DOF. The design uses the nine as follows:

            Field items do not add independent DOF in normal operation: LB-204 and PB-203 are hand bypasses in parallel with LV-204 and PV-203 (the same flows), BV-231 is a block valve in series with TV-231, HV-205 blowdown is an emergency outlet kept shut, and the C-201, CW and steam-block switches are on/off. Each can replace a failed handle, but two handles on one flow must never be adjusted against each other.

            4.2 DOF of each loop

            • A feedback loop uses one DOF: "valve position is free" becomes "CV = SP". The SP is the new free input, given by the operator (or a higher controller).
            • Cascade, ratio and trim add none. The proposed cascade in section 7 (bed-2 peak temperature → TIC-221 SP) still acts through TV-221 alone.
            • A controller in MAN gives its DOF back to the operator. A valve at 0 or 100 % (saturated) loses it: a quench valve wide open can no longer cool its bed, and TV-211 shut can no longer warm bed 1.
            • Two controllers never move one valve at the same time without a selector or split range.

            5 · The control loops on the P&ID

            6 · How the loops were chosen for this P&ID (หลักการกำหนด control loop)

            1. Start from the objectives and the DOF. Nine handles, nine fixed variables: four bed inlets, circulation, make-up, pressure, level and (at design) zero start-up steam.
            2. Pair each CV with the MV that affects it most directly, fastest and with one sign. From the step tests in section 8.4 (OUT +5 % in MAN): TV-221 → bed 2 inlet °C per % with τ ≈ s; TV-211 → bed 1 inlet °C per % (τ ≈ s); PV-203 → loop pressure bar per % (τ ≈ s); C-201 speed → circulation kNm³/h per % (τ ≈ s); LV-204 → level % per minute per % (integrating).
            3. Let the front end set the rate. Make-up also raises the loop pressure, but pairing pressure with make-up would let a pressure controller decide production; the purge is the free outlet, so it holds pressure.
            4. Use fast loops on the handles that carry the heat. Quench and bypass act through gas mixing within seconds, much faster than the catalyst beds heat up, so bed inlets are controlled and bed exits are watched.
            5. Keep safety separate from control. PSHH-203 and LSHH-204 have their own transmitters. TSHH uses the same bed thermocouples as the DCS and FSLL-201 shares FT-201 with FIC-201: a failed element can blind both, which is why FT-201B/FSLL-201B and 2oo3 thermocouples are proposed.
            6. Choose fail positions for the safe state: quench and bypass fail open (cold gas into the beds), make-up, purge, let-down and steam fail closed (no fresh gas, no gas to the let-down drum).
            7. Watch for interaction. Every quench move changes the flow and temperature of the bed below; TIC-211 sits inside the E-201 feedback. The quench loops are tuned so that the lower beds see smooth changes.
            8. Measure where it matters. The bed-inlet elements sit just below each lozenge, after mixing; the analysers on the converter inlet and outlet show composition changes that temperature cannot.
            9. Leave rarely used handles in manual (E-204 steam, field bypasses, blowdown), with alarms and permissives to call the operator.
            Pairing testTV-221 → bed 2 inletTV-211 → bed 1 inletPV-203 → pressureFV-202 → pressureCirculation → bed 2 exit
            Direct effectyes (mixing)yes (mixing)yes (inventory)yes (inventory)indirect (through reaction)
            Sign constantyesyes, but inside the E-201 positive feedbackyesyesno: more gas cools a bed but can also move the reaction
            Gain (step test) °C/% °C/% bar/%+ bar in 1 min for +5 % °C in 1 min for +5 % speed
            DecisionTIC-221TIC-211PIC-203not used: make-up is the plant ratenot used for temperature; FIC-201 holds it constant

            6.1 Interaction seen in the step tests

            • A quench on bed n changes bed n + 1. TV-221 +5 %: the bed-1 flow falls by up to kNm³/h (FI-212), bed 1 exit rises briefly by °C, bed 3 inlet dips by °C before TIC-231 recovers it, and bed 2 exit ends °C lower. TV-241 +5 % lowers bed 4 exit by °C and so the gas that heats E-201.
            • TIC-211 and the E-201 heat balance. TV-211 +5 % in MAN drops the bed-1 inlet by up to °C; bed 1 exit falls °C. Less quench is then needed on bed 2, bed 2 exit ends °C and bed 4 exit °C higher, and the hotter effluent heats the feed again: the inlet recovers to °C below its start. That slow return is the E-201 feedback working against the controller.
            • Pressure and make-up. FV-202 +5 % in MAN: make-up jumps by kNm³/h, then falls back to as the loop pressure rises ( bar in one minute) and the ΔP across FV-202 shrinks. PV-203 +5 %: purge + kNm³/h at the end, production changes by t/h and CH₄ by % as the pressure falls, while FIC-202 holds the make-up (net change kNm³/h).

            Single feedbackMeasure CV, compare with SP, move MV. Corrects any disturbance, but only after it has moved the CV.Base layer almost everywhere.All eight automatic loops
            CascadeThe outer (master) controller sets the SP of an inner (slave) loop on a faster variable; the inner loop removes its own disturbances first. Inner loop 3–5 times faster.A fast disturbance acts on the MV path.Proposed: bed peak temperature (master) → TIC-221 (slave) → TV-221 (figure below). Circulation FIC-201 is already the inner loop for any temperature scheme using flow.

            Feedback trim on a ratioA slow measurement adjusts the ratio.Composition measured but slow.Possible: AI-208 outlet CH₃OH trims the circulation ratio

            Split rangeOne output drives two valves in sequence.One CV needs two handles.Not used; could be PIC-203 on PV-203 then a flare valve

            8 · Control modes: P, PI and PID (แนวทางการควบคุม P, PI, PID)

            The simulator uses the ideal PID form, signals in % of span, derivative on the measurement and an anti-windup clamp:

            OUT(t) = Kc [ e(t) + (1/Ti) ∫e dt − Td dPV/dt ] + bias

            8.1 What each term does

            ModeActionGoodBadTypical use
            POUT change ∝ error now.Simple, immediate.Offset after a load change: e = Δload / (1 + KcK). High gain → oscillation.Averaging level control where offset does not matter.
            PIAdds the accumulated error; keeps moving OUT until the error is zero.No offset. The industrial default.More overshoot if Ti is short; windup when the valve saturates.Flow, pressure, bed temperatures.
            PIDAdds action ∝ rate of change of PV.Helps slow, lag-dominated loops with clean signals.Amplifies noise; kicks on SP changes if taken on error.Rare here: the loops are dead-time small.

            8.2 Guidelines by loop type

            Loop typeModeGainResetDerivative
            Gas flow on valve or speed (FIC-201, FIC-202)PIlow (0.2–1)fast (2–10 s)none
            Bed inlet by quench or bypass (TIC-211…241)PImoderatetens of seconds (real thermowells add lag)none or small
            Gas inventory pressure (PIC-203)PIhighabout a minutenone
            Separator level (LIC-204)PI, averaginglowlong (minutes)none

            8.3 Tuning from a step test (FOPDT model)

            Put the loop in MAN, step OUT, record PV. Fit G(s) = K e−θs/(τs + 1): K = ΔPV/ΔOUT (both in % of span); τ = 1.5 (t63 − t28), θ = t63 − τ. Lambda (IMC) PI: Kc = τ / [|K|(λ + θ)], Ti = τ. For the integrating level, slope K′ (%/s per %) and arrest time λ: Kc = (2λ + θ)/[|K′|(λ + θ)²], Ti = 2λ + θ.

            8.4 Step tests on the model and suggested tuning

            Step tests run on a copy of the model when this tab opens; they do not disturb the running session.

            The temperature loops look very fast (τ of a few seconds) because the bypass and quench act by mixing and the model's thermocouples have no thermowell lag. The simulator's own tuning (Ti 40–60 s) is deliberately slower: in a plant the element adds 20–60 s of lag, and the slow bed and E-201 responses behind the fast mixing make aggressive loops disturb the beds below. The PIC-203 fit shows the opposite: τ of many minutes, so λ = τ is far too slow for a pressure loop.

            9 · Tuning lab (runs the methanol loop model)

            Choose a loop and a test, set the mode and tuning, then Run. The test runs on a copy of the model from design conditions (noise off, SIS active); the dashed line is the simulator's own tuning for comparison. The running session is not affected; to use a tuning live, enter it in the loop's faceplate on the DCS console.

            Loop and test
            Controller
            Presets

            Things to try

            1. TIC-221, load "bed 1 inlet 220 → 224 °C": press P only. The bed-2 inlet settles about 4.9 °C above its set point; with PI (simulator tuning) the offset is gone (peak 1.8 °C, settled in about 13 min).
            2. TIC-211, set-point step: the simulator tuning (1.2 / 60 s) settles in about 6 min. Shorten Ti to 20 s (≈ 1.9 min) and 10 s (≈ 0.8 min); the lambda preset settles in under half a minute. In the model the fast mixing allows this; in a plant the thermowell lag would not.
            3. PIC-203, load "make-up 365.6 → 385": the simulator tuning peaks about 0.6 bar and settles in about 10 min. Kc = 10 halves the peak (≈ 0.3 bar, 2.5 min) but the purge valve swings more; Ti = 600 s lets the pressure rise 0.9 bar and take over 20 min. The lambda preset (λ = τ ≈ 12 min) is far too slow for pressure.
            4. LIC-204, load "make-up 365.6 → 385": P only leaves the level about 1.5 % high; a loose PI (0.5 / 600 s) lets it wander 2.2 % and is not settled after 30 min. For a surge drum that is often what you want: the let-down flow changes smoothly.
            5. FIC-201, set-point step: Kc = 2 with Ti = 1 s overshoots by about 50 kNm³/h (70 % of the 72 kNm³/h step) and the speed swings 75–92 %. Flow loops want moderate gain and a reset near the process time constant (≈ 6 s here).
