            1 Standard and method · 2 Team and documents · 3 Nodes · 4 Guide words and parameters · 5 Risk matrix · 6 Worksheets · 7 Coverage check · 8 Recommendations · 9 Dynamic check on the simulator · 10 Follow-up and close-out

            1 · Standard and method (IEC 61882)

            HAZOP is a structured, team-based examination of a defined system. Each part of the design is compared with its design intent; guide words combined with process parameters generate deviations; for each credible deviation the team records causes, consequences, existing safeguards and, where the risk is not acceptable, recommendations. It finds both hazards (harm to people, environment, assets) and operability problems (the loop cannot make methanol or be run as intended).

            ReferenceWhat it contributes
            IEC 61882:2016 Hazard and operability studies (HAZOP studies) – Application guideDefinitions, the four phases, guide words, team roles, recording
            CCPS Guidelines for Hazard Evaluation Procedures (3rd ed.)Worksheet format, node selection, "consequence without safeguards", risk ranking, links to LOPA
            IEC 61511 (functional safety, SIS)How HAZOP scenarios feed LOPA and SIL targets for the trips I-1 … I-4 and the proposed LSLL-204 / XV-204
            ISO 31000 / owner's risk matrixRisk criteria used to decide whether safeguards are adequate
            API 521 (pressure relief and depressuring), API 941 (steels for hydrogen service), ASME VIIIBasis for PSV-201 / PSV-205 cases, blowdown rate, HTHA material limits and the pressure envelope
            Thailand: Department of Industrial Works regulation on hazard identification, risk assessment and risk-management plans (B.E. 2543)Legal requirement to identify hazards (HAZOP is an accepted method) and to prepare risk-management plans for factories
            OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 (PSM), where applicableProcess hazard analysis for covered processes (methanol, flammable gas above threshold), revalidated at least every five years

            The four phases

            1. Definition: scope from the make-up gas boundary (upstream of XV-202) round the loop to the let-down drum inlet, the purge to reformer fuel and the flare header, including C-201, the SIS (I-1 … I-5) and the E-204 steam and E-203 cooling-water connections; excluded: the front-end syngas compressor, the let-down drum and distillation, the flare system itself. Objectives, team, risk matrix.
            2. Preparation: P&ID, PFD-201 (HAZID tab), heat and material balance (Process tab), cause-and-effect chart (SIS screen), alarm list (Workbook tab), procedures (Exercises tab), datasheets; divide into nodes; write each node's design intent; choose parameters and guide words.
            3. Examination: node → design intent → parameter → guide word → is the deviation meaningful? → causes → consequences assuming the safeguards fail → existing safeguards → rank the risk → recommend → next guide word. Record every meaningful deviation, including those with adequate safeguards ("full recording"), so the reasoning can be audited.
            4. Documentation and follow-up: worksheets, recommendation register with owners and dates, close-out, revalidation after changes (MOC) or periodically.

            2 · Team and documents

            RoleResponsibility
            HAZOP leader (chair)Independent of the design; runs the method, keeps the team on the node, decides when a deviation is covered
            Scribe (recorder)Writes the worksheet live, reads back recommendations
            Process engineer (designer)Design intent, balances, bed temperature limits, catalyst behaviour
            Operations representativeHow the loop is really run: start-up through the SIS, catalyst reduction, upsets, rounds, sampling
            Instrument / control engineerLoops, fail positions, SIS logic, which transmitter each trip uses (independence)
            Safety / risk engineerRisk matrix, LOPA follow-up, relief and depressuring cases
            Specialists as neededCatalyst vendor (reduction, passivation), materials/inspection (hydrogen service), compressor vendor (C-201), maintenance

            Documents for this study: P&ID tab, PFD-201 (HAZID tab), Process tab (stream table and duties), Design tab (limits and sizing), Control loop design tab (loops and fail positions), Workbook tab (alarms and trips), SIS screen (trip logic and permissives), start-up, shutdown and ESD procedures in the Exercises tab.

            3 · Nodes

            A node is a section of the loop with one clear design intent. Boundaries are placed where the intent changes: the make-up valve admits gas, the circulator raises pressure, the interchangers exchange heat, the converter reacts, the cooler condenses, the separator splits liquid from gas, the purge and let-down valves drop pressure. Procedures get their own node (N9) because catalyst reduction, admitting make-up, shutdown and restart create deviations that steady operation does not.

            4 · Guide words and parameters

            Parameters used: flow, pressure, temperature (gas, catalyst and shell), level, composition, heat transfer, integrity (containment), measurement, utility, safety system, material, and for procedures: reduction, admission of make-up, sequence, restart, maintenance, unloading, sampling. A deviation is only recorded if it is physically meaningful ("REVERSE temperature" is not).

            5 · Risk matrix (example for teaching)

            Numbers in brackets: how many deviations of this study fall in the cell. Risk = S × L.

            SSeverity (worst credible consequence)
            1Minor: first aid; small production loss; no release
            2Medical treatment; short outage; small contained release
            3Lost-time injury; loop shutdown for days; catalyst damage; local release
            4Permanent disability or single fatality; major equipment or catalyst loss; fire
            5Catastrophic: multiple fatalities; major fire or explosion; vessel rupture
            LLikelihood with existing safeguards
            1Remote: < 10⁻⁴ /y
            2Unlikely: 10⁻⁴ – 10⁻³ /y
            3Possible: 10⁻³ – 10⁻² /y
            4Likely: 10⁻² – 10⁻¹ /y
            5Frequent: > 0.1 /y

            1–4 Low acceptable · 5–9 Medium reduce if practicable (ALARP), review safeguards · 10–16 High recommendation required, go to LOPA · 20–25 Very high not acceptable, act before operation

            Key scenarios carry the same S × L in the HAZID, HAZOP and Safety layers tabs: gas blow-by through LV-204 S5 × L2 (High, 10); loss of containment of hot H₂/CO/methanol vapour, jet fire S5 × L2 (High, 10); bed temperature runaway (quench valve fails shut, CO-rich gas, loss of circulation with make-up on) S4 × L2 (Medium, 8); CO exposure at sample points S4 × L2 (Medium, 8); pyrophoric reduced catalyst at unloading S4 × L2 (Medium, 8); liquid carry-over into C-201 S3 × L2 (Medium, 6); loop overpressure (purge blocked / PT-203 low) S5 × L1 (Medium, 5).

            6 · HAZOP worksheets (node by node)

            Consequences are written assuming the safeguards fail (worst credible case). S ranks that consequence; L ranks its likelihood with the listed safeguards working as designed.

            7 · Coverage check: guide words applied in each node

            A dot means that guide word gave no meaningful deviation for any parameter in the node (it was still considered). EARLY / LATE / BEFORE / AFTER apply mainly to the procedure node N9.

            8 · Recommendation register

            9 · Dynamic check of selected deviations on the simulator

            A conventional HAZOP judges consequences qualitatively. Here selected deviations are run on copies of the loop model from design conditions with the existing safeguards active (alarms, SIS trips with their 5 s delay, controllers in their normal modes, no operator action) for up to 30 min, or 5 min past a trip. Alarms are evaluated on the model's measurements every second with the page's alarm table and suppression rules. The live session is not touched.

            Runs when this tab is opened.

            What the runs tell the HAZOP team

            • Filled in when the runs finish.

            10 · Follow-up and close-out

            • Each recommendation gets an owner and due date; the owner answers with accepted and done, accepted with alternative (with justification) or rejected (with justification agreed by the HAZOP leader and plant manager).
            • High scenarios whose protection relies on instrumented functions (gas blow-by, loss of containment, bed runaway) go to LOPA (LOPA tab) to set the required SIL for LSLL-204 / XV-204, TSHH 2oo3 and FSLL-201B (IEC 61511).
            • Any change (new catalyst, a higher make-up rate, the agreed additions) goes through management of change, which checks whether the HAZOP must be updated.
            • Revalidate the HAZOP periodically (typically every five years) and after incidents or near misses.
            • Use the simulator to train operators on the scenarios of section 9: the alarm they see first and how much time they have.

            Safety layers · layers of protection for the R-201 methanol converter and synthesis loop

            Teaching slide deck · Safety layers — the six layers, what each adds to the R-201 loop P&ID, the integrity operating window, SIS voting and relief rules.
            Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

            Safety must cover failures of equipment (including control) and of people, and more than one failure at a time. The response should be limited, keeping production where possible. So protection is built in layers, each independent of the others, with more strength held in reserve as the event gets more serious. Source: course 2105625 Process Analysis and Improvement · Process Safety, applied to the methanol synthesis loop. Set points and trip settings are read from the simulator (K, the alarm table, the controllers) when the page opens; values marked "assumed" are for teaching.

            1 The six layers · 2 P&ID layer by layer · 3 What each layer does · 4 Integrity operating window · 5 Independence check · 6 Good practices · 7 Standards

            1 · The six layers (ชั้นป้องกัน 6 ชั้น)

            LayerJobAutomatic?Needs power / computer?Needs a person?
            1 BPCSClosed-loop control keeps the loop in its operating region (bed inlets, circulation, pressure, level)YesYesSupervises
            2 AlarmsBring an unusual situation to the attention of a personNo actionYesYes: decides
            3 SISStop part of the process: make-up gas off (XV-202), C-201 stopped when liquid or ESDYesYes, but de-energise to tripNo (reset only)
            4 ReliefPrevent excessive pressure; send the gas to flareYes, self-actuating (blowdown is manual)NoNo (yes for HV-205)
            5 ContainmentKeep released gas and liquid from workers, community, environmentPassive or remoteMostly noPartly
            6 Emergency responseEvacuation, fire fighting, rescue from CO, health careNoPartlyYes

            Layers 1–4 are the four independent protection layers of the automation. Layers 1–3 all need electrical power, computing and communication, so a power or computer failure could take out all three at once. That is why XV-202 closes with no power (de-energise to trip), why the quench valves TV-221/231/241 and the bypass TV-211 fail open (more cold gas) and FV-202 fails closed (no make-up), and why relief, containment and emergency response are kept in reserve. Click a ring to open that layer on the P&ID.

            Start from the bare process (step 0) and add one layer at a time. Items drawn dashed are recommended additions that are not on MEOH-V1-PID-001 rev A (the same names are used in the HAZOP and LOPA tabs). The drawing is redrawn from the simulator schematic, with the loop spread out so every layer has room.

            Follows the layer selected above.

            4 · Integrity operating window

            Each key variable has a target, alarm limits that still leave time to act, an SIS limit, and a critical limit where damage comes quickly. Green = safe operation, orange = a sustained excursion that must be corrected, red = beyond the critical limit. The arrow is the live value from the simulator: load a training exercise and watch it climb through the layers.

            5 · Independence check

            Each layer must not share its sensor, logic or final element with the layer below; otherwise one failure can defeat both. Alarms that belong to an SIS function may share the SIS sensor, because they sit on the SIS system; a trip that shares the control transmitter is a gap.

            7 · Standards

            • IEC 61511 / ISA-84: SIS life cycle, independence, SIL, proof testing, bypass management. CCPS Layer of Protection Analysis and Guidelines for Safe Automation of Chemical Processes.

            Part A · Reliability for safety

            A1 · Definitions

            TermMeaningOn the R-201 loop
            HazardInherent physical or chemical characteristic that can harm people, environment or property (CCPS)Hydrogen-rich gas at 75–80 bar g and up to 280 °C; an exothermic catalyst bed; CO in the loop gas

            Deterministic / probabilistic analysisCan the design keep events within limits / what is the numerical risk and is it tolerablePSV-201 sized for the worst relief case / LOPA below

            Is 99.9 % reliability good enough? For a 1-in-1000 failure a year it would mean an unsafe landing every day at a big airport. Safety needs both plant reliability (business continuity: 112 t/h of methanol) and safety reliability (hazard prevention and mitigation).

            A2 · Failure rate from a population

            λ = ΔNf / (Ns · Δt): failures in the interval divided by the survivors and the interval length. 100 identical units (think of 100 bed thermocouples across a plant) are drawn from a Weibull life model, R(t) = e−(t/α)β; β < 1 is burn-in, β = 1 the useful life (constant λ = 1/α, the exponential model), β > 1 wear-out.

            A3 · R(t), PFD and proof testing

            With a constant failure rate R(t) = e−λt and PFD(t) = F(t) = 1 − e−λt ≈ λt when PFD ≪ 0.1. A standby safeguard (XV-202 stays open for months) fails unseen, so its PFD grows until the next proof test restores it: PFDavg = (1/T)∫0Tλt dt = λT/2. MTTF = ∫R dt = 1/λ.

            SIL (IEC 61511, demand mode)PFDavgRRF
            SIL 110−2 – 10−110 – 100
            SIL 210−3 – 10−2100 – 1 000
            SIL 310−4 – 10−31 000 – 10 000

            The slider starts at λ = 0.024 /yr: XV-202 with its solenoid (shutdown valve 0.020 + solenoid 0.004, SIS-grade).

            ConfigurationPFDReliabilityFailure rate / MTTFPFDavg over test interval T

            SIF calculator. A safety instrumented function is sensor → logic solver → final element in series; each subsystem can be redundant. Pick one of the loop's trips (I-1 … I-4) or a recommended version, change the voting, the SIS-grade failure rates or the test interval. FV-202 is not part of any SIF: FIC-202 → MAN 0 % is a DCS action, so it takes no credit. Improving reliability: diversity (different technologies), separation (no single point of failure), fail-safe design.

            SubsystemVotingλ per channel (/yr)PFDavgShare

            The course method for parallel systems. Three layers against the same hazard, each with an equivalent failure rate (sum of its blocks), combined as parallel systems through MTTF (inclusion–exclusion): 1/λsys = Σ1/λi − Σ1/(λi+λj) + 1/(λ1+λ2+λ3).

            R-201 bed over-temperature: BPCS = temperature sensor 0.52 + controller 0.2 + quench control valve 0.6; alarm = temperature sensor 0.52 + controller 0.2 + operator 1.0; SIS = SIS temperature sensor 0.002 + logic solver 0.001 + shutdown valve XV-202 0.020 + solenoid 0.004. The result is set by the most reliable branch. LOPA (Part B) treats the same layers differently: it multiplies the demand rate by each layer's PFD, and it gives no credit to a layer that shares a component with the initiating event or with another credited layer.

            A5 · Failure data used in this tab

            EquipmentFailure mode / contextGeneric rate (/yr)SIS / safety-grade rate (/yr)

            Sources used by the course: OREDA and the CCPS Guidelines for Initiating Events and Independent Protection Layers. A generic rate counts all failure modes; an SIS rate counts only dangerous undetected failures of certified equipment. For a control valve or transmitter that must fail in one direction to start a scenario, half the generic rate is used (assumed). The C-201 motor stop rate is assumed.

            Part B · Layers of protection analysis (LOPA)

            B1 · The method

            1. Take a scenario from the HAZOP (cause → consequence) and rate its severity; the severity sets the target frequency.
            2. Estimate the initiating event frequency (IEF) from failure data. If several causes lead to the same consequence, work each and add the frequencies.
            3. Credit each independent protection layer (IPL) with its PFD. A layer that shares a component with the initiating event, or with another credited layer, gets no credit. An alarm needs enough time (typically ≥ 10 min) for the operator to act.
            4. Apply enabling events (time at risk) and conditional modifiers (probability of ignition, occupancy, probability the consequence develops).
            5. Compare with the target: RRF = f / target. If RRF > 1, the gap sets the PFD, and so the SIL, of the extra layer.

            Lecture example: pressure control malfunction 0.1 /yr × high-pressure alarm 0.1 × relief valve 0.01 × occupancy 0.1 = 10−5 /yr against a fatality target of 10−6 /yr → RRF = 10, not acceptable.

            B2 · Criteria used here (course risk matrix)

            SeverityTarget risk frequency (/yr)Health and safetyEnvironmentEconomic

            Likelihood levels by frequency: 5 most likely (~10 /yr), 4 likely (~1), 3 possible (~0.1), 2 rare (~0.01), 1 almost impossible (~0.001); the band boundaries are taken halfway between decades. Risk = severity × likelihood: 1 negligible, 2–6 low, 8–12 medium, 15–20 high, 25 extreme. Target frequencies differ by country (for a fatality about 10−4 to 10−6 /yr). This matrix is stricter than the HAZID/HAZOP ranking bands (R = S × L, 10–16 High). The severities are the ones agreed for the whole OTS: gas blow-by S5, loop overpressure S5, bed runaway S4, carry-over into C-201 S3.

            B3 · What counts as an IPL

            An IPL must be independent of the initiating event and of the other credited layers, specific to the scenario, dependable (its PFD can be justified) and auditable (tested). Procedures, training and inspection are safeguards but usually not IPLs. On this loop every SIF ends on the same valve XV-202 and the same logic solver SIS-201, so two SIFs cannot both be credited in one scenario.

            LayerPFD credited

            B4 · R-201 loop LOPA worksheet

            Part C · Bow-tie

            A bow-tie is several LOPAs drawn around one top event (the moment control of the hazard is lost). Threats on the left pass prevention (control) barriers; consequences on the right sit behind recovery (mitigation) barriers and conditional modifiers. Escalation factors are conditions that defeat a barrier (a bypass, a plugged nozzle). The top-event frequency is the sum of the threat frequencies times their barrier PFDs. Barrier colours follow the Safety layers tab; grey is a procedure or a conditional modifier. A barrier marked "shares sensor" gets no credit while the barrier it shares with is working.

            Escalation factors

              1 · What a cause and effect diagram is

              • A cause is one sensed condition with its direction and setting (low, low-low, high, high-high, push-button, permissive not met). Alarm-only causes light the amber alarm and sound the horn; trip causes act on the final elements and raise the red SIS alarm.
              • An effect is one action on one device or latch, written as a code in the header row (C close, S stop, TP tripped, F first-out, A activate, P permissive, RB reset blocked). A mark shows which causes drive it.
              • The matrix follows the SRS of each SIF (the SRS of SIF tab) and the alarm list, and must match the logic exactly. Here the effects are read from the simulator's trip functions, and section 5 tests them on a copy of the model.

A transition is the planned change between one condition and another.                   1 · What a transition is, and which ones this loop has

                  Transitions are planned transient behaviour between different initial and final conditions. The loop was designed for its steady state, so each transition needs its own procedure and strategy. Some also need extra equipment that is idle in normal running.

                  Kind (lecture)When it happensOn the R-201 loopPart

                  Done before the procedure starts (lecture list, applied to this loop):

                    3 · Cold start-up: the order and the reasons

                    No.StepWhy this order (analysis)Safety concern

                    3.1 Heating the catalyst with E-204

                    Before any make-up gas is admitted, loop gas is circulated through E-204 to heat the catalyst to its light-off temperature. The runs below start from the cold loop (30 °C, 40 bar g of loop gas, C-201 stopped). C-201 is started, TIC-211 is set to 225 °C, and the E-204 steam valve HIC-214 is set to different openings. The plot shows the time to reach the 200 °C permissive on TI-211 and TI-212.

                    3.2 Admitting the make-up gas: how fast?

                    The runs below use the same heat-up, then open XV-202 with FIC-202 in MAN at 4 %. The quench loops are put in AUTO. The FIC-202 output is then raised at 1, 3 or 10 % per minute, or stepped to 50 % or 80 %. The rest of the script follows the proven procedure. E-204 steam is cut back once the bed-1 exit passes 235 °C. When the loop reaches 72 bar g, FIC-202 goes to AUTO and its set point moves 30 kNm³/h per minute to 366. All trips are armed.

                    Events in the selected run

                    4 · Shutdown: stop the heat source first, keep the heat sink running

                    No.StepWhy this order (analysis)Safety concern

                    Events in the selected run

                    5 · Blocked-in operation and the hot restart

                    A short outage of the front end (reformer, syngas compressor) does not need a full shutdown. The make-up is stopped and the loop is swept briefly. C-201 is then stopped, leaving the loop blocked in under pressure with the catalyst hot. This is hot standby. The beds lose heat only slowly, so the restart skips most of the heat-up. The runs start from the model's hot-standby state after 2, 8 and 24 h blocked in and follow the hot-restart procedure (C-201 at 1000 kNm³/h, E-204 if bed 1 is below 205 °C, FIC-202 output +2 % per minute while every bed is below 268 °C).

                    6 · Catalyst change, reduction and other maintenance transitions

                    Cu/ZnO/Al₂O₃ catalyst slowly loses activity as copper crystallites sinter and poisons (sulfur, chlorine) accumulate. It is replaced every few years. The lecture gives three strategies for units that must regenerate or be maintained: parallel equipment, storage so the neighbours keep running, or shutdown. This loop has one converter, so a catalyst change is a planned shutdown. A crude-methanol tank lets the distillation unit keep running for part of it, and lets the loop keep running when distillation is down.

                    TransitionWhyWhat changesHazards and how they are handledStrategy

                    6.1 Reducing fresh catalyst (typical practice, not in the model)

                    The catalyst is delivered as CuO/ZnO/Al₂O₃ and must be reduced in the converter: CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, ΔH ≈ −80 kJ/mol (exothermic, assumed value). Typical practice is to circulate nitrogen at low pressure through E-204 and heat the beds slowly to about 150–170 °C. Hydrogen is then added a little at a time, starting at about 0.5–1 % in N₂. The temperature rise across each bed is watched and kept small. The H₂ is raised in steps only when the exotherm dies down, and the final hold is at about 210–230 °C. The water formed is condensed in E-203 and drained from V-201; it is the measure of progress. The simulator starts from reduced catalyst, so this calculator uses assumed values (labelled).

                    Adiabatic rise: ΔT ≈ yH₂ × |ΔH| / cp,N₂, with cp ≈ 29.5 kJ/(kmol K), if all the H₂ reacts in the bed. Circulation is given as a share of design flow ( kNm³/h). Nitrogen at low pressure gives much less volume flow than synthesis gas, so a lower share is realistic. All values are assumed; follow the catalyst vendor's procedure.

                    6.2 How big must the crude-methanol storage be?

                    If distillation stops, the loop can keep running only while a tank takes the crude: V = F × t / ρ. The tank must be held nearly empty in normal running to give that space. The opposite case also works: a full tank lets distillation run on while the loop is down for a catalyst change.

                    7 · Rate changes: the front end sets the rate

                    The loop takes whatever make-up the front end sends, so every change of plant rate is a transition for the loop. This is load following, and there is no storage for syngas. The runs below start at design and raise the FIC-202 set point from 366 to 415 kNm³/h in one step or as a ramp, with every loop in AUTO:

                    Lecture's industrial practice (steam supply)Same idea on this loop

                    8 · Feed-composition changes from the front end

                    When the reformer changes its operation, the make-up composition changes, even at the same flow. CO releases more heat than CO₂ when it forms methanol (about −98 against −58 kJ/mol, with the shift reaction). A CO-rich gas therefore heats the beds, bed 1 first. The runs below ramp the make-up to CO-rich over 10 minutes (CO 16 → 21 %, CO₂ 7 → 5 %) at the same flow. Three responses are compared: no action; the bed-inlet set points moved at 1 °C/min to °C after the TI-214 high alarm; and the same move made as soon as the front end announces the change.

                    9 · End-of-run moves as the catalyst ages

                    Over a catalyst life of several years, activity falls. Operators compensate slowly by raising the bed-inlet temperatures, which is a very slow, planned transition. The table shows steady states from the model (Operating windows engine, trips off) for catalyst ageing 0 to 1 (1 = −60 % activity) and inlets raised 0, 5 and 10 °C from 220/225/230/235.

                    10 · Batch operation, and what makes transitions hard

                    Batch and semi-batch processes never reach a steady state, so every batch is a transition. The R-201 loop is continuous; its transitions are the ones above.

                      Process reliability · how long the R-201 loop runs between outages, and how to make it run longer

                      Teaching slide deck · Process reliability — reliability, failure rate and availability; series, parallel, standby and k-out-of-N structures on the methanol loop; the loop as a series system; design and operation for reliability; catalyst life, inventory, maintenance and life-cycle cost.
                      Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

                      Follows the course material on reliability: T. Marlin's Operability in Process Design, Chapter 4 Reliability, and the Introduction to Reliability Engineering course (failure statistics, MTTF/MTBF, series, parallel and k-out-of-N models, critical items). The LOPA tab treats the reliability of safeguards, as a probability of failure on demand. This tab treats the reliability of production: here an outage costs money, not lives. Failure rates are the course's generic all-modes values where one exists. Fractions, repair times and costs marked "assumed" are teaching values. Restart times come from the Transition operation tab's model runs.

                      1 Definitions · 2 Failure rate and life · 3 Structures · 4 The loop as a series system · 5 Design for reliability · 6 Operating for reliability: catalyst life · 7 Inventory · 8 Maintenance · 9 Life-cycle cost · 10 Reliability audit

                      1 · Reliability, availability and why they differ

                      TermDefinitionOn the R-201 loop

                      Availability is not reliability. A loop that trips eight times a year but restarts hot in half an hour each time has high availability and poor reliability. Every trip is a restart, a temperature cycle on the catalyst and a load of syngas to flare. The course example: three years of the same plant with uptimes of 6815, 7612 and 8471 h out of 8760 h.

                      2 · Failure rate, the bathtub and the exponential model

                      The failure rate λ(t) is the number of failures per unit time divided by the items still working. Over a lifetime it often follows the bathtub: infant mortality (λ falling), chance failures (λ constant) and wear-out (λ rising). Most real equipment does not follow the full bathtub; the RCM studies found six patterns, most with no wear-out. The right maintenance depends on the pattern. With constant λ:

                      R(t) = e−λt,   F(t) = 1 − R(t),   MTTF = 1/λ

                      At t = MTTF only 37 % of items survive (63.2 % have failed). The course example: λ = 0.0001 /h gives MTTF 10 000 h, R(5000 h) = e−0.5 = 0.61, and 0.5 expected outages in 5000 h.

                      3 · Structures: series, parallel, standby, k out of N

                      A plant is many components joined in structures, and the structure sets the system reliability. All formulas here assume independent failures (no common cause) and, for standby, perfect switching.

                      StructureWorks whenReliabilityMTTF (identical elements, λ each)Example on this loop

                      four identical elements at λ = 4 × 10⁻³ /h: MTTF 62.5 h in series, 521 h in parallel, 1000 h as one running plus three standby.

                      A standby is only as good as its switch-over time. The chapter's warning fits this loop exactly. When C-201 stops, FSLL-201 trips the make-up once the circulation has been below 45 % of design for 5 s (the model's trip delay). No operator can start a spare circulator in 5 s, and a large machine cannot run up to speed that fast by itself. A spare circulator therefore shortens the outage (a switch-over instead of a repair) but cannot prevent the FSLL trip unless it starts automatically within the 5 s trip delay, which in practice means a spare already spinning (hot standby) or a longer trip delay that the LOPA must accept.

                      4 · The loop as a series system: what stops it, and how often

                      To produce methanol every element in the chain must work: front end → make-up valves → C-201 → exchangers → R-201 → E-203 → V-201 → trips, plus utilities. The loop is therefore a series system: λsys = Σ λi × fi, where fi is the fraction of element i's failures that stop the loop (a spurious trip, a lost machine, a leak). Each outage lasts the repair time plus a restart. The restart is taken from the Transition operation runs: hot restart to line-out h after a short stop, h after 24 h blocked in, and a cold start-up h (simulator time; a real cold start takes much longer). Tick design changes and see the effect.

                      5 · Design for reliability

                      Lecture principleWhat it meansR-201 loop as builtGap or recommendation

                      "There is no safe side in equipment sizing." An oversized machine runs far from its best-efficiency point. For a centrifugal circulator that means recycle, surge margin problems, vibration, and seal and bearing failures. An oversized control valve works near its seat and wears there. The same holds for catalyst: loading far more than needed lowers the bed temperatures at start of run. It costs pressure drop and circulation power every day for a margin used only at end of run.

                      6 · Operating for reliability: short-term gain against catalyst life

                      The lecture's turbo-generator trade-off applies here too: running hotter raises efficiency now, but above a limit the failure rate climbs. On R-201 the trade-off is the hottest-bed temperature. Hotter beds give more methanol on aged catalyst (Transition tab, part 9), but copper crystallites sinter faster and the catalyst life shortens. Moving a variable toward a constraint must be combined with reducing its variability.

                      Rule of thumb, assumed for teaching: the sintering rate doubles for every 15–20 °C of hottest-bed temperature, so relative life = E[2−(T − Tdesign)/ΔTd] over the operating distribution of T. Tdesign is the model's hottest catalyst at design ( °C). Real deactivation also depends on poisons, water partial pressure and the CO₂/CO ratio.

                      7 · Reliability through inventory

                      A tank between an unreliable unit and the next lets the next unit keep running while the first is repaired. With the upstream unit's repair time exponentially distributed (mean MTTR) and a holdup time τ = V/F, the chance that one outage is covered by the tank is 1 − e−τ/MTTR. Then R = R₂[R₁ + (1 − R₁)(1 − e−τ/MTTR)]. The lecture's example uses P1 reliability 0.15 and P2 reliability 0.95. On this plant the crude-methanol tank sits between the loop (upstream) and distillation (downstream). There is no syngas storage between the front end and the loop.

                      Inventory has a price: working capital, the tank itself, a flammable inventory of crude with dissolved gases, and product that may degrade. The chapter's Tables 4.1 and 4.2 list the reasons for and against. The engineer places inventory next to the unreliable units and sizes it for their repair times.

                      8 · Maintenance for reliability

                      Strategy (NASA RCM)IdeaItems on this loop that suit it

                      9 · Life-cycle cost: one circulator or two?

                      Life-cycle costing adds to the usual profitability analysis the costs that reliability changes: maintenance and spares, failure frequency, the cost of each failure (repair, lost production, restart, flared syngas) and the extra equipment for redundancy. The lecture's example asks how many pumps to install; here the question is whether C-201 should have a spare. The lost margin per hour defaults to the page's profitability model at design (training prices). Costs are assumed teaching values. Restart times come from the Transition operation tab.

                      1 · Efficiency, optimisation and their place among the priorities

                      Efficiency (in operation, the same as optimisation) is good economic performance: more product from the same raw material, less energy per tonne, less effluent and a lower environmental impact. For a methanol loop the raw material is carbon, so the headline number is the carbon efficiency = carbon leaving as methanol ÷ carbon entering in the make-up gas (CO + CO₂ + CH₄). Energy is tracked as specific energy (kWh of circulator power per tonne) and as the heat of reaction that is recovered, rejected or lost.

                      Four ways to get it (lecture): design with the right capacities; use the existing equipment in its most efficient way; choose better process structures (recycle, recover heat, recover hydrogen); choose the best operating conditions inside the window. Efficiency is the sixth priority: it is pursued only inside the limits that protect people, the environment, the equipment, smooth operation and quality.

                      PriorityObjectiveOn the R-201 loop

                      Chains multiply

                      Each step of the route from make-up carbon to saleable methanol keeps only part of what it receives, so the efficiencies multiply. The first two links are the live simulator; the third (the distillation unit, outside this model) is an assumed value you can change.

                      2 · The loop's efficiency now: direct and indirect method

                      Direct method: carbon efficiency = carbon in the crude methanol (XI-210 ÷ 32.04) ÷ carbon in the make-up. Indirect method: 100 % − losses, where the losses are the carbon that leaves as CO, CO₂ and CH₄ in the purge and the blowdown. The indirect method is what plants use when the product flow is less reliable than the gas analyses. Both are computed from the running simulator every second; the difference between them is shown and explained, not hidden.

                      3 · Loop pressure: equilibrium and rate against compression

                      Typical practice: a higher synthesis pressure raises the per-pass conversion (four moles of gas become two, so equilibrium and the rate both move toward methanol). Here PIC-203 holds the separator pressure by opening the purge; its set point was swept from 70 to 80 bar g with the make-up held at 365.6 kNm³/h.

                      4 · Circulation: more methanol, more power

                      Typical practice: more circulation (a higher recycle ratio) lowers the per-pass conversion but raises the production, because the converter sees more reactant and the beds run cooler; the price is circulator power, which rises roughly with the cube of the flow. FIC-201 was swept from 1500 to 2400 kNm³/h at a constant make-up.

                      5 · Separator temperature: every degree leaves methanol in the recycle

                      Typical practice: each °C of separator temperature leaves more methanol vapour in the recycle gas (its vapour pressure rises about 3 % per °C at 40 °C). That methanol is not lost; it goes back to the converter, where it pushes the reaction back toward equilibrium, and part of it leaves in the purge. The cooling-water supply to E-203 was swept from 28 to 40 °C; the separator follows about 8 °C above it.

                      6 · Bed temperatures and catalyst age

                      A bed inlet that is too cold wastes catalyst (slow kinetics); one that is too hot runs into equilibrium sooner and sinters copper. There is an optimum, and it moves as the catalyst ages. The bed 4 inlet (TIC-241) was swept at design activity; the catalyst-ageing runs compare the design inlets with all four inlets raised 10 °C.

                      Bed 4 inlet sweep: all numbers

                      7 · The purge, and improvement options sized for this loop

                      The purge carries the inerts out of the loop, and with them hydrogen, some CO and CO₂ and a little methanol vapour. It goes to the reformer as fuel, so it is not wasted, but a fuel credit is worth much less than the same carbon or hydrogen made into methanol. Set the prices (defaults are the page's Profitability prices) and the assumed recoveries:

                      8 · Best operating conditions: push toward the constraints

                      Many conditions do not affect safety or quality but do affect profit; the best value is usually against a constraint. Here the two handles are circulation (limited by C-201 speed, 95 % in the operating window) and loop pressure (limited by the PIC-203 high alarm, 78 bar g, with the PSHH-203 trip at 85 bar g and PSV-201 at 88 bar g behind it). The table is the model's margin over a grid of both; the slider below shows how close to the alarm a pressure set point can sit for a given variability.

                      Industrial practice: optimise slowly (one handle at a time, let the loop settle for 20–30 minutes before the next move: the loop inventory and the catalyst have long time constants); use the model where there is one and careful plant tests where not; reduce variability first, then move the set point toward the limit.

                      9 · Energy monitoring: key energy variables of the loop

                      A plant energy dashboard tracks the specific consumption (energy or raw material per tonne of product) against its benchmark and the key energy variables (KEV) that move it. Live from the simulator; the "effect" column comes from the model sweeps above.

                      1 What an SOP is · 2 Format · 3 SOP register · 4 SOP viewer · 5 Writing rules · 6 Life of an SOP

                      1 · What an SOP is, and which activities need one

                      A standard operating procedure is the written, approved way to carry out one task: the same steps, in the same order, with the same checks, whoever is on shift. It turns the reasons worked out on the other tabs (heat-up before make-up, the operating window, the bounds, the SIS trips) into actions an operator can follow under pressure, at 3 a.m., with alarms sounding.

                      Required by process safety management, OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(f): written procedures for each operating phase — initial start-up, normal operation, temporary operation, emergency shutdown (including the conditions that require it and who decides), emergency operation, normal shutdown, start-up after a turnaround or an emergency shutdown; the operating limits, the consequences of deviation and the steps to correct or avoid it; safety and health considerations (properties and hazards of the chemicals, exposure precautions, PPE, control measures); and the safety systems and their functions. They must be readily accessible, reviewed as often as needed and certified annually as current, and trained on; safe work practices (lockout/tagout, line opening, confined space, control of entry) are part of the same clause.

                      6 · The life of an SOP

                      Draft from the design intent and the hazard studies (HAZID, HAZOP, LOPA) → verify on the simulator (the graded procedures in the Exercises tab run the same steps against the same model) → review by operations, process, safety and, for the SIS steps, instrumentation → approve and train (read, walk through, practise on the simulator) → use, reporting every deviation → review after any change (management of change: a new tag such as the recommended XV-204 or FT-201B changes several SOPs), after an incident, and at the fixed interval (certified annually under 1910.119(f)(3)).

                      References: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 (f) Operating procedures; CCPS, Guidelines for Writing Effective Operating and Maintenance Procedures (1996); CCPS, Guidelines for Safe Process Operations and Maintenance (1995); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 (control of hazardous energy, lockout/tagout); Thai Department of Industrial Works notification on process safety management (B.E. 2543).
